judge_assessment.explanation: Both hard failures are exact. Every one of problems 2 through 5 opens with a diagnosis instruction before it asks for a number: problem 2 'Name the error, then find the correct length of TU'; problem 3 'Explain why a factor greater than 1 cannot be right here, then find ED'; problem 4 'Name what Rae scaled incorrectly, then find the correct area'; problem 5 'State which two lengths Ines paired that do not correspond, then find the correct height h'. verify.json holds seven entries: ids 1 through 5 are a single solve/approx apiece with a numeric expected (12, 21, 6, 128, 27.5), id 6 has an approx (12) plus one manual entry. So the named diagnosis -- the thing the prompt calls the focus, 'diagnosing reversed correspondence or scale-factor errors' -- is recorded on exactly one of the six problems, and that one only because part (c) happens to be the numeric part. The second claim is likewise verifiable by count: exactly one manual entry exists in the whole file. The judge's numbers all recompute (EF=12, TU=21, ED=6, larger area 128, flagpole 27.5, KL/NP=12), and the traps line up with the planted wrong values printed in the stems. REJECT is correct.

strengths_to_preserve: The trap declarations are the model of what the prompt asked for and should be preserved verbatim as a pattern. Every planted wrong result printed in a stem has a matching `traps` entry with the expression that produces it and its value -- Kai's 9.33 = 14*10/15, Rho's 13.5 = 9*12/8, Rae's 80 = 50*8/5, Ines's 17.6 = 4*22/5, Tomas's 33.33 = 20*15/9 -- so the wrong answer is machine-checked as distinguishable from the right one, not merely asserted in prose.

The answer key's 'Common wrong answers' block is generated from those traps and states the misconception in one line each ('paired the flagpole's shadow with the person's height, reversing the correspondence'). A grader seeing 17.6 on a page knows immediately which error produced it.

Problem 3 deliberately scrambles the similarity statement (triangle ABC similar to triangle FED, with the sheet telling the student to 'read that statement carefully'), so the correspondence cannot be recovered by alphabetical pattern-matching. That is the single most effective way to make reversed correspondence visible, and it is used once rather than repeated into a gimmick.

The directions teach a prediction habit before any arithmetic: 'Before computing, decide which triangle is larger; then say whether your answer should be bigger or smaller than the side you started from.' Problem 6 then makes that habit the whole question -- explain why Tomas's answer is impossible BEFORE any arithmetic is checked.

root_causes.description: SKILL.md's guidance on error-analysis actively steers the author away from a manual entry. Line 249 says to reframe understanding topics as checkable tasks and specifically covers 'error-analysis ("find and fix the mistake") via the ordinary types -- the planted wrong result is checkably wrong and the correction checkably right', while line 257 says to use `manual` for 'any explanation/reasoning answer'. On a find-and-fix item both apply, and the first is the one written in the voice of an instruction for this exact problem shape. The author followed it, encoded the correction as `approx` plus a trap, and never added the manual companion for the diagnosis.
evidence: SKILL.md line 249: 'error-analysis ("find and fix the mistake") via the ordinary types -- the planted wrong result is checkably wrong and the correction checkably right'
SKILL.md line 257: 'Use `manual` for ... any explanation/reasoning answer'
verify.json ids 2, 3, 4, 5: approx entries with traps, no manual companion, despite each stem opening with 'Name the error' / 'Explain why' / 'Name what' / 'State which'
final_response.md presents six machine checks and one manual item as the intended boundary

root_causes.description: A declared trap proves the WRONG value is distinguishable; it does not record that the student named the error. The two are different responses and the contract has no way to say so, so a trap reads to every gate as full coverage of a find-and-fix item.
evidence: verify.json id 2 trap desc 'wrote the scale factor upside down, shrinking a side of the larger triangle' -- the author's diagnosis, not the student's
worksheet problem 2 prints two responses: the named error and TU; only TU is checked
gate_log.txt reports verify-ws MANUAL with a single manual item, and every other gate PASS

improvements.title: A find-and-fix item's named diagnosis needs a manual entry alongside its corrected value
improvements.proposed_change: Rewrite the SKILL.md line-249 error-analysis sentence so it stops implying that ordinary types discharge a find-and-fix item. New wording: the CORRECTION goes in an ordinary type with a declared trap; the DIAGNOSIS ('name the error', 'explain why this is wrong') is an explanation and takes a companion `manual` entry under the same id, with the expected diagnosis in `desc`. Enforce it in scripts/verify.py: any id that carries a `traps` array and no `manual` entry exits 2 with a message naming the id. That single rule catches ids 2, 3, 4 and 5 here and generalises to every misconception-analysis case in the suite.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture verify JSON with {"id": 1, "type": "approx", "expr": "14*15/10", "expected": 21, "traps": [{...}]} and no manual entry for id 1; assert verify.py exits 2 and its output names problem 1. Today it exits 0 for that id, which is the defect.
improvements.expected_impact: Restores an honest manual boundary on the entire misconception-analysis mode. On this sheet it moves five of six problems inside the boundary instead of one, and the trap-plus-manual pairing becomes the canonical encoding for the format.
improvements.risk: Low. The rule keys on a field the author already writes deliberately, so false positives are rare -- a trap without a diagnosis instruction is an unusual sheet, and exit 2 costs one line of review rather than a rebuild.

improvements.title: Count the printed responses on each find-and-fix item, not just the corrected number
improvements.proposed_change: Have tests/check_layout.py count response slots per \problem segment and fail when the count exceeds the entries carrying that id. On this sheet each of problems 2 through 5 prints two responses (a named error and a corrected value) against one entry, and problem 6 prints three -- (a) which triangle is larger and why, (b) the rule for orienting the factor, (c) the correct NP -- against two, where the single manual entry's desc covers (a) and (b) together. Splitting that manual entry into one per lettered part makes the answer key's grading note addressable part by part.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture problem printing a diagnosis instruction and a numeric request with a single approx entry for its id; assert check_layout.py exits non-zero naming the uncovered slot. Silent today.
improvements.expected_impact: Makes the coverage gap visible at build time on every mixed diagnosis-plus-correction item, rather than at judging time.
improvements.risk: Medium. Prose slots have no macro to count, so the checker must key on imperative markers in the stem; expect tuning against the eval corpus before it becomes a hard gate.

case_summary: This sheet does the hardest part of the misconception-analysis format better than anything else in my batch: every planted wrong result printed in a stem has a matching declared trap with the expression that generates it (9.33, 13.5, 80, 17.6, 33.33), the key's 'Common wrong answers' block is generated from them, and problem 3's deliberately scrambled statement (ABC similar to FED) defeats alphabetical pattern-matching. All six corrected values recompute (12, 21, 6, 128, 27.5, 12). The rejection is nonetheless right and the mechanism is diagnosable: SKILL.md line 249 tells the author to encode error-analysis 'via the ordinary types', which is true of the correction and false of the diagnosis, so 'Name the error', 'Explain why', 'Name what Rae scaled incorrectly' and 'State which two lengths Ines paired' -- the focus the prompt names -- are recorded nowhere, and exactly one manual entry exists in the whole file. A declared trap proves the wrong value is distinguishable; it does not record that the student named it.
